name: Resveratrol topical
lead: Resveratrol (3,5,4'-trihydroxy-trans-stilbene) is a plant polyphenol found in grape skins, berries and peanuts, and in knotweed root used for supplements [1]. Applied to the skin, it appears in anti-aging and brightening cosmetics, where it is marketed as an antioxidant [1].

Much of the published topical work concerns delivery: resveratrol has low water solubility and is photosensitive, and researchers have tested nanocarriers, emulsions and gels to improve skin retention [2][3][4]. Human evidence on appearance is sparse. An 8-week randomized placebo-controlled trial in healthy women over 40 reported reduced visible signs of skin aging with trans-resveratrol [5], and small registered trials of resveratrol-containing products exist [6][7]. Wikipedia's general resveratrol article states that there is no significant evidence of an effect on aging skin [1].

paras: Topical resveratrol is used in products aimed at wrinkles, uneven pigmentation and general skin aging [1][5]. It has also been tested in formulations aimed at psoriasis, burn wounds and skin cancer in laboratory and animal settings [8][9][4].

Oral bioavailability of resveratrol is described as about 0.5 percent because of extensive metabolism, with a very short half-life of parent compound [1]. This is one reason research has turned to the skin as a route and to carriers that raise skin retention: chitosan/gum Arabic Pickering emulsions increased cutaneous retention and lowered permeation in porcine skin ex vivo, and also improved photostability [2]. Nanostructured emulsions raised transdermal deposition in another study [3].
The general resveratrol article reports adverse effects, mainly gastrointestinal, with long-term high oral intake; it does not describe topical adverse effects [1].

An 8-week randomized placebo-controlled trial published in Frontiers in Aging in 2025 tested trans-resveratrol in healthy women over 40 and reported reductions in visible signs of skin aging [5]. A registered early phase 1 trial of topical extract and other nutraceuticals for wrinkles and pigmented spots has unknown status (n=25) [6]. A phase 4 trial of a resveratrol-containing product in acne was terminated (n=43) [7]. Evidence is limited to these small studies.

card.summary: An antioxidant stilbene sold in anti-aging serums, with one small recent trial and mostly delivery-formulation research behind it.
card.note: Poorly stable and poorly absorbed; human skin evidence is a few small studies.

quick.overview:
Topical resveratrol is a plant antioxidant used in anti-aging and brightening skincare. Research so far has centered on how to get it into skin and keep it stable.

One 8-week randomized trial in women over 40 reported fewer visible signs of aging, but the human evidence base is small.
quick.mechanism: It is marketed as an antioxidant. Studies on delivery show nanocarriers and emulsions can raise how much stays in the skin in laboratory models.
quick.risks: The sources describe no topical adverse-effect data; reported side effects of resveratrol are mainly gastrointestinal with high oral intake. It is light sensitive and degrades easily.
